pos: adj. (rude and ungenerous; hard in dealing; the character of Nabal)
etymology: From Old English ceorl, a common freeman, which drifted into meaning a boor. The Authorized Version uses it once, of Nabal the Carmelite, who is introduced as churlish and evil in his doings in the same sentence that praises his wife.
biblical_def: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings. The contrast is the hinge of the chapter. David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds in the wilderness and asked at sheepshearing for whatever came to hand; Nabal's answer is a small masterpiece of self-regard, with the pronoun repeated: Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be? Abigail intercepted four hundred armed men with loaves, wine, sheep, parched corn, raisins, and figs, and with a speech that named her husband honestly — as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him — and that recalled David from a slaughter he had sworn to commit. David's reply is the verdict on the whole episode: Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me. Nabal's heart died within him ten days later, and the LORD smote him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): rude; surly; austere; sullen; rough in temper; unfeeling; uncivil; also, selfish; narrow-minded; avaricious.
webster_full: CHURLISH, a. Rude; surly; austere; sullen; rough in temper; unfeeling; uncivil.
CHURLISH, a. Selfish; narrow-minded; avaricious.
CHURL, n. A rustic; a countryman or laborer; a rough, surly, ill-bred man.
LIBERALITY, n. Largeness of mind; catholic principles; generosity; munificence.
FOLLY, n. Weakness of intellect; imbecility of mind; want of understanding; in Scripture, criminal weakness; depravity of mind.
scriptures: Now the name of the man was Nabal; and the name of his wife Abigail: and she was a woman of good understanding, and of a beautiful countenance: but the man was churlish and evil in his doings; and he was of the house of Caleb.
Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.
And David said to Abigail, Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, which sent thee this day to meet me:
corruption_summary: Ungenerous hardness is defended as prudence and as a right over one's own property; Scripture names Nabal's reasoning folly and puts his name on it, while commending the wife who acted over his head to prevent bloodshed.
corruption_paragraphs: Nabal's refusal was legally unimpeachable. The bread was his, the water was his, the flesh was killed for his shearers, and he owed David nothing by contract. Scripture calls him a man of Belial and folly all the same, because the biblical doctrine of property has never been absolute ownership. The land was the LORD's, the corners of the field belonged to the poor by statute, and the whole law assumes that a man's goods are held in trust with obligations attached. My bread, my water, my flesh, is the grammar of a fool, and the chapter says so.

Abigail's part requires care and the dictionary gives it plainly. She acted without telling her husband, contradicted his decision, and is commended by David and by the narrator. Submission in Scripture is never a mandate to assist in sin or to stand by while blood is shed; Abigail intervened to prevent a massacre and to keep David from avenging himself, and she did it with humility, courage, and remarkable theological skill, reminding him that the LORD would make him a sure house and that he should not have this as a grief of heart, that thou hast shed blood causeless. Her example is the standing answer to anyone who reads headship as a licence for folly.

pos: adj. (belonging to a child; and so immature where maturity is owed)
etymology: From child with the adjectival ending. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's account of the difference between what he was and what he became: when I became a man, I put away childish things.
biblical_def: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things. The verse sits inside the chapter on charity, and it is an argument about the present age. Paul has just said that prophecies shall fail, tongues shall cease, knowledge shall vanish away, for we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. Childhood is his figure for now, and manhood for then, and the next verse completes it: for now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. The dictionary therefore takes the verse as eschatology before it is ethics, and only then as ethics. Where Scripture does apply childishness morally it is careful about which direction: Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men. Innocence of malice is to be kept and the thinking is to grow up. Ephesians names the danger of failing to: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): belonging to a child; trifling; puerile; ignorant; silly; in Scripture, what a man puts away on becoming a man.
webster_full: CHILDISH, a. Belonging to a child; trifling; puerile.
CHILDISH, a. Ignorant; silly; weak; not becoming a man.
PUERILE, a. Boyish; juvenile; trifling; as puerile amusements.
MATURITY, n. A state of ripeness; completion; the state of being complete, perfect or finished.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things.
scriptures: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
Brethren, be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men.
Eph 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
corruption_summary: Doctrinal seriousness is treated as a hardening that maturity should soften, and simplicity of faith is confused with simplicity of mind; Paul commands the opposite, that Christians be children in malice and men in understanding.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 14:20 separates two things the church habitually confuses. In malice be ye children — keep the incapacity for spite, the absence of grudge-keeping, the artlessness. In understanding be men — grow up in doctrine, in judgment, in the ability to weigh a claim. The common failure inverts both: congregations sophisticated in suspicion and infantile in theology. Hebrews rebukes exactly that in people who ought to have been teachers and still needed milk, and says that strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.

Ephesians names what immaturity costs. Children are tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive. The remedy Paul gives is not less doctrine but more, delivered by pastors and teachers, until we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man. And the manner is fixed in the same paragraph so that the growing up never becomes contempt: speaking the truth in love.
roots_summary: Greek nepios (G3516), an infant, a child, one without speech; teleios (G5046), complete, full-grown; katargeo (G2673), to put away or render inoperative.
roots_lines: Greek nepios (G3516) — an infant, a babe, and so childish; when I was a child.
Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature, full-grown; that which is perfect.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render idle, to abolish, to put away; I put away childish things.
Greek kakia (G2549) — malice, badness; in malice be ye children.
Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by waves; tossed to and fro.

“in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” — the two directions.
“tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine” — the cost of not growing.

pos: adj. (of or from the devil; the third and worst description of false wisdom)
etymology: From devil, Greek diabolos, an accuser or slanderer, with the adjectival ending. The Authorized Version uses it once, at the climax of James's description of a wisdom that does not descend from above.
biblical_def: This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish. The three adjectives are a descent. Earthly — belonging to this world and reaching no higher. Sensual — of the natural man, driven by what he feels and wants. Devilish — of the same source as the accuser himself. James has just identified the material this wisdom works with: if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, glory not, and lie not against the truth. And he states the result without qualification: for where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work. It is a striking claim about church conflict. Not merely that envy is wrong, but that it is a wisdom with a pedigree, and the pedigree runs downward. Against it James sets the alternative in one of the most complete descriptions of sanctified character in the New Testament: but the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Pure first, and peaceable second, and in that order.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): partaking of the qualities of the devil; diabolical; malicious; in Scripture, the last of three descriptions of the wisdom that is not from above.
webster_full: DEVILISH, a. Partaking of the qualities of the devil; diabolical; very evil and mischievous; malicious.
SENSUAL, a. Pertaining to the senses; carnal; not spiritual or intellectual.
EARTHLY, a. Pertaining to the earth, or to this world; worldly; belonging to our present state.
ENVY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; in Scripture, true religion, godliness, piety.
scriptures: Jas 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
Jas 3:14
But if ye have bitter envying and strife in your hearts, glory not, and lie not against the truth.
Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
Jas 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
corruption_summary: Envy and rivalry inside the church are treated as personality friction to be managed, when James traces them to a wisdom that is earthly, sensual, and devilish, and says they produce confusion and every evil work.
corruption_paragraphs: James refuses to let congregational conflict be described as a clash of temperaments. He asks in the next chapter, from whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? and answers his own question with desire, envy, and unanswered asking. That is a spiritual diagnosis of what usually gets a procedural remedy. Confusion and every evil work is a heavy phrase for a church dispute, and it is deliberately heavy, because a disordered congregation is not merely inefficient; it is displaying a wisdom with the wrong ancestry.

The remedy offered is not a technique but a character, and its order is instructive. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable. A peace bought by surrendering purity is not the wisdom from above but a counterfeit of it, which is why the dictionary will not treat unity as the highest good in a dispute about truth. Yet the rest of the list gives no shelter to the quarrelsome: gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace of them that make peace.
roots_summary: Greek daimoniodes (G1141), demon-like, devilish; psuchikos (G5591), of the natural soul, sensual; akatastasia (G181), confusion or tumult.
roots_lines: Greek daimoniodes (G1141) — resembling a demon, devilish; the one occurrence, James 3:15.
Greek psuchikos (G5591) — of the natural life or soul, sensual; the middle term of the descent.
Greek epigeios (G1919) — belonging to the earth, earthly; the first term.
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, and so envy or jealousy; bitter envying in your hearts.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — instability, confusion, tumult; there is confusion and every evil work.

“where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” — the result.
“first pure, then peaceable” — the order of the true wisdom.

etymology: From head; one who goes headlong. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the catalogue of the character of men in the last days, between traitors and highminded.
biblical_def: Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God. The word falls in the middle of a list of eighteen or nineteen traits that Paul gives Timothy as the marks of perilous times: lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God. The list begins with self-love and ends with pleasure-love, and every item between is a species of one or the other. Then comes the clause that makes the passage a church matter rather than a cultural one: having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. Paul is not describing the pagan world outside. He is describing a religion that keeps its shape and loses its force, and his instruction to the young minister is not to argue with it but to withdraw from it. The times are called perilous, and the peril is inside the form.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): rash; hasty; precipitate; violent; disposed to rush forward without deliberation; headstrong.
webster_full: HEADY, a. Rash; hasty; precipitate; violent; disposed to rush forward in an enterprise without thought.
HEADSTRONG, a. Violent; obstinate; ungovernable; resolute to run his own way.
HIGHMINDED, a. Proud; arrogant; in Scripture, thinking of oneself more highly than one ought.
TRAITOR, n. One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one who betrays his trust.
APOSTASY, n. An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith.
scriptures: Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
corruption_summary: The catalogue of 2 Timothy 3 is read as a description of the unbelieving world, when Paul attaches it to those having a form of godliness and denying the power, and tells Timothy to turn away from such.
corruption_paragraphs: Every item on Paul's list can be found in any society in any century, and Christians habitually read the chapter as a commentary on the culture. The fifth verse redirects it. Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away. These are people with a religion. They have the shape — the vocabulary, the attendance, the profession — and the power that would make it change them has been denied, whether by outright unbelief or by a practical refusal of it. That is what makes the times perilous. A frankly pagan age is dangerous; an age of hollow religion is more dangerous, because the form disguises the absence.

The instruction Paul gives is unusually blunt and worth keeping: from such turn away. Not argue, not accommodate, not build a bridge — turn away, and get on with what he charges Timothy with in the same letter, which is to continue in the things he has learned, to know the holy scriptures, and to preach the word, be instant in season, out of season. The chapter that diagnoses a hollow religion prescribes the Scriptures, given by inspiration of God and profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.

“lovers of their own selves” — where the list begins.

pos: n. (sleepiness; heaviness with sleep; the companion of the drunkard and the glutton)
etymology: From drowse, Old English drusian, to sink or become sluggish. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Proverbs, where drowsiness clothes a man with rags.
biblical_def: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags. Proverbs groups three appetites that all end in the same place, and the third is the one nobody confesses. Drunkenness and gluttony are recognisable sins; drowsiness feels like nothing at all, and Proverbs gives it the same destination. The book returns to it repeatedly and always with the same gentle mockery: yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep, so shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man. The poverty is not sudden. It walks toward a man at the pace of a traveller while he sleeps, and then arrives armed. And the sluggard is addressed directly: How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Paul takes the figure into the Christian's waiting for his Lord and turns it eschatological: and that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): sleepiness; heaviness with sleep; disposition to sleep; dullness; sluggishness.
webster_full: DROWSINESS, n. Sleepiness; heaviness with sleep; disposition to sleep.
DROWSY, a. Inclined to sleep; sleepy; heavy with sleepiness; dull; stupid.
SLUGGARD, n. A person habitually lazy, idle and inactive; a drone.
SLOTH, n. Slowness; tardiness; disinclination to action or labor; sluggishness; laziness; idleness.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
scriptures: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
Pro 6:11
So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.
And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
corruption_summary: Sloth is reclassified as rest and self-care and so removed from the list of sins entirely, when Proverbs sets it beside drunkenness and gluttony and gives it the same end.
corruption_paragraphs: The old moralists counted sloth among the deadly sins and modern speech has almost no word for it. Rest is a creational good, commanded in the fourth commandment and modelled by God himself, and the dictionary will not let a doctrine of diligence swallow the Sabbath or turn exhaustion into a virtue. But Proverbs is not describing rest. It is describing a man who will not plow by reason of the cold, who turns upon his bed as the door turneth upon his hinges, who hides his hand in his bosom and it grieveth him to bring it again to his mouth, and who is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. The humour is affectionate and the verdict is not.

Paul's use moves the whole figure into the Christian life without dropping the practical edge. It is high time to awake out of sleep, the night is far spent, the day is at hand; let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light. Watchfulness is the New Testament's posture for the church between the ascension and the return, and the parable of the ten virgins turns on lamps and sleep. Drowsiness in Scripture is finally a failure to reckon with the time.

pos: adj. (dissatisfied; uneasy in mind; bitter of soul)
etymology: From dis- and content, Latin contentus, held within bounds. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the men who gathered to David in the cave Adullam.
biblical_def: And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. David has escaped to the cave Adullam, and the men who come to him are the least promising army in Scripture: the distressed, the indebted, and the bitter of soul. These four hundred became six hundred, and out of them came the mighty men whose names 2 Samuel records one by one — the three who broke through the host of the Philistines to fetch him water from the well of Bethlehem, and the man who slew a lion in a pit in time of snow. Grace makes something of what it gathers. The dictionary takes the cave as a picture of the church, which has never been assembled out of the qualified, since God hath chosen the weak things of the world, and not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called. What the bitter men in the cave needed, and slowly learned under a captain who would not lift his hand against the LORD's anointed, is what Paul says he had to learn as well: I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): uneasy in mind; dissatisfied; unquiet; in Scripture, describing the men who gathered to David at Adullam, bitter of soul.
webster_full: DISCONTENTED, a. Uneasy in mind; dissatisfied; unquiet.
DISCONTENT, n. Want of content; uneasiness or inquietude of mind; dissatisfaction at any present state of things.
CONTENTMENT, n. Rest or quietness of the mind in the present condition; satisfaction which holds the mind in peace.
MURMUR, v.i. To grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half articulated voice.
ADULLAM, n. A city of Judah; also, the cave in which David took refuge.
scriptures: And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men. was in
David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Discontent is validated as an authentic response to circumstance and left there, when Scripture treats contentment as something learned, rooted in a promise, and taught to bitter men in a cave.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul's statement about contentment is remarkable chiefly for the verb. I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. It is not a temperament he happened to have and not a state he arrived at once; he says elsewhere in the same paragraph that he learned both how to be abased and how to abound, both how to be full and to be hungry. Contentment in the New Testament is an acquired competence, taught by God through circumstances, and the strength for it is named: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

Hebrews gives the ground rather than the technique, and the ground is a promise about a Person, not a change in the circumstances: let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. That is the whole argument. The reason a Christian may be content with what he has is that he cannot be left by the One who has him. The men in the cave were in real distress and real debt, and nothing in the text minimises it; what changed them was a captain worth following and a God who kept his word about a throne.

pos: n. (shameful conduct; in 2 Corinthians, the hidden things a minister renounces)
etymology: From dis- and honesty, Latin honestas, honour or decency; the Greek behind it means shamefulness. The Authorized Version uses it once, where Paul names what he and his fellow workers have renounced.
biblical_def: But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. Paul is defending a ministry under suspicion at Corinth, and the defence is a description of method. Three things renounced: the hidden things of shame, craftiness in walking, and the deceitful handling of the word of God. One thing put in their place: the plain setting forth of the truth, offered to every man's conscience, in God's sight. The last phrase governs the rest, because a man who works in the sight of God has no use for the hidden things. And the chapter goes on to strip the messenger out of the message entirely: for we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. Then the frailty is conceded rather than hidden: but we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. Paul is content to be a clay pot, because a clay pot cannot take credit for what it carries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): want of probity or integrity in principle; faithlessness; a disposition to defraud or deceive; in Scripture, the shameful hidden things a minister renounces.
webster_full: DISHONESTY, n. Want of probity, or integrity in principle; faithlessness; disposition to cheat or defraud.
DISHONESTY, n. Violation of trust or of justice; fraud; treachery; any deviation from probity.
CRAFTINESS, n. Cunning; artfulness; stratagem; artifice.
MANIFESTATION, n. The act of disclosing what is secret, unseen or obscure; discovery to the eye or to the understanding.
SINCERITY, n. Honesty of mind or intention; freedom from hypocrisy.
scriptures: But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost:
corruption_summary: Persuasion is pursued by technique — managed impressions, selective preaching, pressure applied at the right moment — where Paul renounces craftiness and rests the whole enterprise on the open setting forth of the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Handling the word of God deceitfully covers more than lying about it. It includes the selective text, the omitted clause, the sermon pitched to what a room will pay for, and the pressure applied by a technique rather than by the truth. Paul's alternative has no lever in it at all: by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. He states the case and leaves the result with God, and the next verse says plainly that some will not receive it — if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost.

The reason he can preach that way is given in the same paragraph and it is a doctrine, not a temperament. The god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not; and the God who commanded the light to shine out of darkness has shined in our hearts. If unbelief is blindness, no technique can cure it and no crafty handling is worth attempting; if God gives the light, then the plain truth plainly told is exactly the instrument he uses. Craftiness in ministry is finally a confession that one does not believe this, and the earthen vessel is the proof that one does.
roots_summary: Greek aischune (G152), shame, shamefulness; panourgia (G3834), craftiness, unscrupulous cleverness; doloo (G1389), to adulterate or handle deceitfully.
roots_lines: Greek aischune (G152) — shame, disgrace; the hidden things of dishonesty.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — craftiness, cunning, readiness for anything; not walking in craftiness.
Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, to falsify; nor handling the word of God deceitfully.
Greek phanerosis (G5321) — a manifestation, an open showing; by manifestation of the truth.
Greek ostrakinos (G3749) — made of clay, earthen; this treasure in earthen vessels.
usage: “have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty” — the single occurrence.
“we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord” — the content settled.
“this treasure in earthen vessels” — the vessel conceded.

pos: adv. (unwillingly; with reluctance; literally, out of grief)
etymology: From grudge, Old French grouchier, to murmur. The Greek behind the Authorized Version's word is literally of grief — giving out of sorrow at the giving. It occurs once.
biblical_def: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. Paul is arranging the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, and the whole of 2 Corinthians 9 is about how the money is to be given rather than how much. Three things are excluded: grief at the giving, compulsion from outside, and the sparing calculation that hedges — he which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. What is required is purpose in the heart and cheerfulness in the act, and the Greek word for cheerful is the one English gets hilarious from. The promise attached is not a promise of wealth but of sufficiency for further giving: God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work. The chapter ends where all Christian giving has to end, with the gift no one could match or repay: Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): unwillingly; with reluctance; in Scripture, the manner of giving which God does not accept, set against the cheerful giver he loves.
webster_full: GRUDGINGLY, adv. Unwillingly; with reluctance; with discontent.
GRUDGE, v.i. To be discontented at another's enjoyments or advantages; to envy; to be unwilling to give.
CHEERFUL, a. Lively; animated; having good spirits; full of life and gladness.
LIBERALITY, n. Munificence; bounty; a particular act of generosity; a gift.
STEWARDSHIP, n. The office of a steward; the management of another's property.
scriptures: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:
Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.
corruption_summary: Giving is either extracted by pressure and guilt or promised back with interest as an investment; Paul forbids compulsion, forbids grief in the giving, and promises sufficiency for further good works rather than gain.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite abuses of this chapter are common in the modern church. The first is the pressure appeal — the emotional squeeze, the public pledge card, the implication that a reluctant giver is not a real Christian. Paul excludes it in four words: not grudgingly, or of necessity. He would not even take the Corinthians' collection as a matter of commandment, saying he spoke not by commandment but to prove the sincerity of their love. The second abuse is the prosperity appeal, which reads sow bountifully and reap bountifully as an investment contract with God. The reaping Paul names in the next verse is all sufficiency in all things so that you may abound to every good work — enough, so that you can give again.

The chapter's foundation is not a technique of fundraising but a fact. He that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness. The giver is giving what he was given, and the increase is God's doing. That is why cheerfulness is the fitting manner: a man who understands that he is passing on a gift has nothing to grieve over in the passing. Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift — the sentence the whole appeal rests on and ends with.
roots_summary: Greek lupe (G3077), grief or sorrow, in the phrase rendered grudgingly; hilaros (G2431), cheerful; anagke (G318), necessity or compulsion.
roots_lines: Greek lupe (G3077) — grief, sorrow, pain; literally, not of grief — rendered grudgingly.
Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful, joyous, propitious; God loveth a cheerful giver.
Greek anagke (G318) — necessity, constraint; nor of necessity.
Greek proaireomai (G4255) — to purpose beforehand, to choose; as he purposeth in his heart.
Greek anekdiegetos (G411) — unspeakable, indescribable; his unspeakable gift.
usage: “not grudgingly, or of necessity” — the single occurrence.
“for God loveth a cheerful giver” — the manner required.
“Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift” — where the appeal ends.

pos: n. (persistent and shameless asking; the quality commended in the friend at midnight)
etymology: From Latin importunus, troublesome, inconvenient; the Greek word carries the sense of shamelessness. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the Lord's parable of the friend who knocks at midnight.
biblical_def: I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth. A man goes to a neighbour at midnight because a traveller has arrived and he has nothing to set before him, and the neighbour answers through a bolted door that the children are in bed. The Lord's point is not that God is reluctant. It is an argument from the lesser to the greater, the same shape as the unjust judge who avenged the widow to be rid of her: if even a grudging man will answer shameless persistence, how much more will a Father answer his children. The application follows immediately: And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. Then the comparison is made explicit and the gift named: If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? Luke sets the other parable of persistence with the same purpose stated at its head: men ought always to pray, and not to faint.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): pressing solicitation; urgent request; application for a claim or favor which is urged with troublesome frequency or pertinacity.
webster_full: IMPORTUNITY, n. Pressing solicitation; urgent request; application for a claim or favor, which is urged with troublesome frequency.
IMPORTUNE, v.t. To request with urgency; to press with solicitation; to urge with frequent or unceasing application.
PERSEVERANCE, n. Persistence in any business or enterprise undertaken; continuance in a state of grace to a state of glory.
SUPPLICATION, n. Entreaty; humble and earnest prayer in worship.
PARABLE, n. A fable or allegorical relation or representation of something real in life or nature, from which a moral is drawn.
scriptures: Luk 11:8
I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth.
Luk 11:9
And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?
Luk 18:1
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
corruption_summary: Persistent prayer is turned into a technique that wears God down, or abandoned on the reasoning that a sovereign God needs no asking; the parable argues from a reluctant neighbour to a willing Father, and the Lord commands the asking.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable is regularly read backwards, as though God were the sleeping neighbour and prayer a matter of persistence overcoming reluctance. The logic is the reverse. Both of Luke's parables on prayer work by contrast: a grudging friend, an unjust judge who feared not God neither regarded man — and then, shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. The persistence is commanded because the Father is willing, not because he is not.

The opposite error reasons that since God has decreed all things, asking changes nothing. Scripture never draws that conclusion and the Lord who taught most plainly about the Father's sovereign will also taught most insistently about asking. Prayer is one of the appointed means by which what God has decreed comes to pass, which is why James can say, ye have not, because ye ask not. And the gift named at the end of this passage is the measure of the Father's willingness: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him.
roots_summary: Greek anaideia (G335), shamelessness, importunity; aiteo (G154), to ask; ekkakeo (G1573), to faint or lose heart.
roots_lines: Greek anaideia (G335) — shamelessness, bold persistence; the one occurrence, Luke 11:8.
Greek aiteo (G154) — to ask, to request; Ask, and it shall be given you.
Greek zeteo (G2212) — to seek, to search for; seek, and ye shall find.
Greek krouo (G2925) — to knock; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to lose heart, to grow weary; pray, and not to faint.
usage: “yet because of his importunity he will rise” — the single occurrence.
“Ask, and it shall be given you” — the application the Lord draws.
“men ought always to pray, and not to faint” — the other parable's stated purpose.

pos: n. (settled ill-will; a disposition to put the worst construction on everything)
etymology: From Latin malignitas, ill-nature, from malus, bad. The Greek word means a bad disposition, the habit of taking things in the worst sense. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's catalogue of the fruits of a mind given over.
biblical_def: Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers. The list belongs to the argument of Romans 1, and the structure around it matters more than any single item. Three times Paul says that God gave them up or gave them over — to uncleanness, to vile affections, and finally: even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient. The catalogue that follows is what a mind looks like when God has withdrawn his restraint, and malignity sits in it between deceit and whispering, in the company of the quieter sins. The paragraph ends at the worst point: who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them. And then, without a chapter break in the argument, Paul turns on the reader who has been agreeing: Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): extreme enmity or evil dispositions of heart towards another; malice; a disposition to put the worst construction on words and actions.
webster_full: MALIGNITY, n. Extreme enmity, or evil dispositions of heart towards another; malice; extreme malevolence.
MALIGNITY, n. Evilness of nature; as the malignity of fraud.
WHISPERER, n. One who whispers; a tale-bearer; a secret slanderer.
REPROBATE, a. Not enduring proof or trial; abandoned in sin; lost to virtue or grace.
CENSORIOUS, a. Addicted to censure; apt to blame or condemn; severe in making remarks on others.
scriptures: Rom 1:29
Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers,
Rom 1:28
And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;
Rom 1:32
Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them.
Rom 2:1
Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
corruption_summary: Romans 1 is read as a list of other people's sins, which is the precise use Paul anticipates and demolishes in the sentence immediately following it.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter division here has done real damage, because Paul's argument does not pause. He builds a catalogue that any moral reader will applaud — and then turns: therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest. The list was a trap for the self-righteous, and the quieter sins in it are the teeth. Envy, debate, deceit, malignity, whispering, backbiting, boasting, disobedience to parents, covenantbreaking, unmercifulness — these are respectable-church sins, and they are in the same sentence as murder. A man who reads Romans 1 and thinks only of the culture has read it exactly as Paul feared.

Malignity itself deserves naming for what it is: not an outburst but a settled bent, the habit of assuming the worst about a person's motive and construing every ambiguous act against him. It is the opposite of the charity of 1 Corinthians 13, which thinketh no evil and believeth all things. It thrives in congregations because it never has to be confessed — it looks like discernment from the inside. The remedy is the one Romans supplies three chapters later: there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, which is a fact a malignant heart cannot hold and stay malignant.
roots_summary: Greek kakoetheia (G2550), malignity, bad character, the habit of putting the worst construction on things; adokimos (G96), reprobate, rejected after testing; psithuristes (G5588), a whisperer.
roots_lines: Greek kakoetheia (G2550) — bad disposition, malignity; the one occurrence, Romans 1:29.
Greek adokimos (G96) — failing the test, rejected, reprobate; God gave them over to a reprobate mind.
Greek psithuristes (G5588) — a whisperer, a secret slanderer; next in the list.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to hand over, to deliver up; God gave them over.
Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse, inexcusable; thou art inexcusable, O man.
usage: “deceit, malignity; whisperers” — the single occurrence, among the quieter sins.
“God gave them over to a reprobate mind” — the judgment the list illustrates.
“Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest” — the turn.
